title: Oral Rehydration Salt and Oral Rehydration Therapy
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders
Oral Rehydration Salt and Oral Rehydration Therapy

headings.title: Introduction to Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) and Dehydration
headings.content: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) is one of the most significant medical breakthroughs of the twentieth century, drastically reducing morbidity and mortality rates associated with acute diarrheal diseases, particularly in resource-limited settings across Nigeria. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid and electrolytes than it takes in, often triggered by viral or bacterial gastroenteritis leading to profuse vomiting and watery diarrhea. In infants and young children, dehydration can progress rapidly from mild to severe, resulting in hypovolemic shock, renal failure, and death if prompt fluid resuscitation is not initiated. ORT involves the simple yet scientifically grounded administration of fluids by mouth to prevent or correct the electrolyte and water deficits associated with dehydration. Understanding the pathophysiology of dehydration enables nursing students to recognize early clinical signs such as lethargy, sunken fontanelles, dry mucous membranes, and decreased skin turgor. By prioritizing oral rehydration over immediate intravenous access when appropriate, nurses can safely and effectively restore circulating blood volume and electrolyte balance, avoiding the complications associated with invasive venous cannulation in pediatric and adult patients alike.

headings.title: Physiological Mechanisms and the Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter
headings.content: The efficacy of Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) relies entirely on sophisticated physiological mechanisms operating within the mucosal lining of the small intestine, specifically the sodium-glucose linked transporter (SGLT1). Under normal conditions, secretory diarrhea causes massive losses of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen, overwhelming absorptive capacities. However, sodium and glucose absorption are tightly coupled in the brush border of enterocytes. The SGLT1 cotransporter actively transports one molecule of sodium and one molecule of glucose simultaneously across the apical membrane into the cell, driven by an electrochemical gradient maintained by the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase pump. Crucially, this transport mechanism remains completely intact and functional even during severe secretory diarrhea caused by pathogens like Vibrio cholerae or rotavirus, which typically inhibit other ion transport pathways. As sodium and glucose move intracellularly via SGLT1, an osmotic gradient is created, pulling water passively across the tight junctions and cellular membranes into the extracellular fluid and bloodstream. This remarkable physiological synergy underpins why adding glucose to oral sodium solutions transforms plain water into a life-saving rehydration fluid.

headings.title: Composition and WHO Guidelines for Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS)
headings.content: To maximize safety and efficacy, the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF established standardized formulations for Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS). The updated, low-osmolarity ORS formulation contains a reduced concentration of both glucose and sodium, which significantly decreases stool output, lowers the incidence of vomiting, and reduces the need for unscheduled intravenous fluid infusions compared to older, higher-osmolarity preparations. A standard WHO-recommended low-osmolarity ORS packet is formulated to be dissolved in one liter of clean drinking water and typically contains sodium chloride (2.6 g), glucose anhydrous (13.5 g), potassium chloride (1.5 g), and trisodium citrate dihydrate (2.9 g), yielding a total osmolarity of approximately 245 mOsm/L. The inclusion of potassium helps replace intracellular losses and prevent hypokalemia, while citrate acts as a buffer to correct metabolic acidosis frequently associated with severe diarrheal illnesses and dehydration. Nurses must educate caregivers on the absolute necessity of using the correct volume of clean water when mixing ORS powders, as incorrect dilution can lead to hypernatremia or inadequate rehydration, both of which pose serious clinical risks to vulnerable patients.

headings.title: Pharmacokinetics and Mechanism of Action of ORS
headings.content: The pharmacokinetics of Oral Rehydration Salts focus on the rapid dissolution, gastric transit, and intestinal absorption of water, sodium, potassium, and glucose. Once ingested, the solution rapidly empties from the stomach into the duodenum, where the osmolality and chemical composition facilitate immediate action via the SGLT1 pathway. Glucose and sodium are absorbed in an equimolar or near-equimolar fashion, generating an osmotic pull that draws free water from the intestinal lumen into the enterocytes and subsequently into the mesenteric microcirculation. This rapid restoration of intravascular volume improves renal perfusion, corrects electrolyte imbalances, and buffers systemic pH through the action of the bicarbonate precursor, citrate. The mechanism of action is entirely local to the gastrointestinal tract and systemic through extracellular fluid expansion; it does not rely on hepatic metabolism or complex enzymatic breakdown. Nurses must understand that ORS does not magically stop the underlying infectious diarrhea itself—rather, it sustains the patient's hydration status and physiological stability while the immune system clears the pathogen or specific antimicrobial therapy takes effect.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Assessment of Dehydration Severity
headings.content: Accurate clinical assessment of dehydration severity is paramount for determining whether a patient requires home management, clinic-based oral rehydration therapy, or emergency intravenous resuscitation. Clinical assessment tools, such as the WHO classification system, categorize dehydration into three distinct categories: No Dehydration, Some Dehydration, and Severe Dehydration. Patients with 'No Dehydration' exhibit normal behavior, alert mental status, moist eyes, and tears, with normal skin pinch return. 'Some Dehydration' is characterized by restlessness or irritability, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, a thirsty demeanor, and a skin pinch that goes back slowly (between two seconds). 'Severe Dehydration' represents a medical emergency marked by lethargy or unconsciousness, very sunken and dry eyes, inability to drink or drink poorly, and a skin pinch that goes back very slowly (longer than two seconds), often accompanied by cold, moist skin and feeble pulses. Nurses must perform thorough head-to-toe assessments, taking vital signs and monitoring weight changes, to ensure appropriate triage and timely execution of therapeutic protocols.

headings.title: Administration Guidelines and Preparation Protocols for Nurses
headings.content: Proper administration and preparation protocols for ORS are critical nursing responsibilities that directly influence treatment success. Nurses must ensure that one entire packet of WHO ORS is mixed precisely into the recommended volume of water—typically one liter, or the exact fraction indicated on smaller packets—using a clean container and clean measuring device. Water quality is vital; ideally, boiled and cooled water should be used, or safe drinking water from an unpolluted source to prevent secondary infections. Once mixed, the solution must be covered and used within 24 hours, after which any remaining solution should be discarded to prevent bacterial contamination. During active rehydration for patients with 'Some Dehydration', the calculated target amount of ORS should be administered over a four-hour period, offering frequent, small sips using a cup and spoon rather than a feeding bottle, which can introduce infection or cause aspiration. If an infant vomits, the nurse should instruct the mother or caregiver to wait ten minutes and then resume feeding slowly, giving a spoonful every two to three minutes while continuing to monitor fluid intake and output closely.

headings.title: Contraindications, Precautions, and Adverse Effects
headings.content: While ORS is remarkably safe, nurses must be vigilant regarding contraindications, precautions, and potential adverse effects during administration. Absolute contraindications for oral rehydration therapy include severe dehydration with hemodynamic instability (which necessitates immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation), severe shock, intestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, and patients experiencing intractable vomiting that prevents any oral intake. Precautions must be taken with patients suffering from impaired renal function or severe heart failure, as excessive sodium or fluid loads can precipitate fluid overload or electrolyte imbalances. Adverse effects are rare when ORS is prepared correctly, but hypernatremia can occur if the solution is mixed with too little water or if inappropriate, high-solute homemade drinks are substituted. Conversely, hyponatremia can develop if plain water is given in massive quantities without adequate sodium replacement. Nurses must monitor serum electrolytes, urine output, and neurological status to catch early warning signs of electrolyte derangements, such as twitching, confusion, or lethargy.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Education in ORT
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing interventions and patient education are the cornerstones of successful outpatient and inpatient ORT management. Nurses play a vital educational role by teaching mothers and caregivers how to recognize signs of worsening dehydration, how to properly mix and store ORS, and the importance of continuing age-appropriate feeding, including breastfeeding, throughout the diarrheal episode. Nutritional support is vital; food should not be withheld, as early feeding maintains gut integrity, shortens illness duration, and prevents malnutrition. Furthermore, nurses should promote preventative health measures, such as hand hygiene, safe sanitation practices, exclusive breastfeeding for infants under six months, and the administration of zinc supplements as recommended by public health guidelines to reduce the severity and recurrence of future diarrhea episodes. Documentation of intake and output, daily weights, and serial physical assessments ensures continuity of care and allows the multidisciplinary healthcare team to evaluate treatment efficacy and modify interventions proactively.
